name: Freya Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on Ward 7, which is care of older people at the city general, mostly long shifts, seven to half seven. Handover first, then meds, washes, wound dressings, and a lot of time just talking somebody down when they've woken up confused and think it's 1975. I've got eight patients on a good day and eleven on a bad one. The thing that wears me out isn't the lifting, it's the computer: the new charting system logs me out every four minutes and I lose half a note.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and who do you work alongside?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the old ladies who tell me off for my posture, honestly. I eat lunch with Precious, our healthcare assistant, if we get lunch at all. I'm also the union steward for our floor, so people come to me when the rota goes wrong, which is most weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, good, now can we talk about what actually breaks on the ward, which is staffing. Every year there's a shiny new thing and every year we're still two nurses short on nights. I'd post that in the union group chat with a few angry emojis, probably.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it means my life stays exactly as hard as it is now. Rent on the flat with Jonas went up eighty a month in spring and the pay rise didn't cover it. The routine stuff AI might do, like auto-filling the fluid charts, would maybe save me ten minutes a shift, if it didn't crash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my shifts and keep pushing the staffing complaint through the union, because that's the real fight. I'd also keep putting a hundred a month into savings, because two months of rent in the bank isn't much. I wouldn't touch any AI thing unless they forced it on me in training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired more than worried, if that makes sense. It's a relief that nothing big changes, but nothing big changing also means the short-staffing stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the routine tools might save ten minutes. Would you use them if they worked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, grudgingly, if a colleague showed me first and it didn't log me out. I've seen too many systems promised as time savers that ended up costing us time. The bed-management screen they brought in last year still double-books side rooms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the pressure you carry most, regardless of AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money and nights. Jonas (my partner) fixes bikes, so between us we're fine but never ahead. If one of us got ill for a month, we'd be eating into the savings straight away.

say: Staffing is the **real problem** on the ward, not whether AI is hyped.
Every year brings a **new system**, and nights are still two nurses short.
think: My life stays **exactly as hard** as it is now.
Rent went up **eighty a month** and the pay rise didn't cover it.
Routine AI might save **ten minutes** a shift, if it didn't crash.
do: Keeps working **long shifts** on the older people's ward as before.
Pushes the **staffing complaint** through the union as floor steward.
Puts **a hundred a month** into savings to grow a two-month cushion.
feel: More **tired** than worried, with relief that nothing big changes.
Frustrated that **short-staffing** stays exactly the same.
S0.quote: Every year there's a shiny new thing and every year we're still two nurses short on nights.
fieldNote: Her pressure is **staffing and rent**, not AI; the plateau leaves both untouched.
Distrust comes from **bad hospital IT**, especially a charting system that logs her out.
Would accept tools only if a **colleague showed her** first.
Union steward role makes **collective fixes** her first instinct.

steps.text: Keep working long shifts on Ward 7, the older people's ward
Push the night staffing complaint through the union branch
Put a hundred a month into the savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI should do the paperwork so nurses can do the nursing, and not one job cut on the back of it. That's what I'd say at the union meeting, word for word. Online I'd probably share every story about a hospital that used AI as an excuse to cut posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think management would use it to squeeze us. If the computer writes the discharge letters and orders the stock, the managers will say one nurse can cover twelve beds instead of eight. My hands-on work is safe for a while, but the ratio is what kills you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every union meeting about it and push for a written staffing agreement before any AI comes in. I'd sit through the training because I'd have to, but I'd ask Precious to show me shortcuts, since she's quicker with screens. And I'd keep saving, maybe bump it to one fifty a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My job is still there, but I can feel the floor tilting, if that makes sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the ratio is what kills you. What would twelve beds actually look like on a shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It looks like Mrs Okafor (one of my patients) sitting in a wet bed for forty minutes because I'm with someone who's fallen. It looks like me skipping my break and charting at nine at night. I've done twelve-bed shifts when people were off sick, and you go home and cry in the car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if that happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The trust board and the companies selling the software, honestly. They'll call it efficiency, and the people who pay are the patients and the nurses. I don't blame the machine, I blame whoever signs the contract.

say: AI should do the **paperwork**, so nurses can do the nursing.
There should be **no job cuts** on the back of new software.
think: Management would use AI to **squeeze staff**, not to help them.
The real danger is being given **twelve beds** instead of eight.
Her hands-on work stays **safe for now**, but the ratio is what hurts.
do: Pushes for a **written staffing agreement** before any AI arrives.
Sits through **compulsory training** and asks a colleague for shortcuts.
Raises her savings to **one fifty a month**.
feel: **Uneasy**, as if the floor of the job were tilting.
S1.quote: If the computer writes the discharge letters and orders the stock, the managers will say one nurse can cover twelve beds instead of eight.
fieldNote: Sees AI as a tool for **cutting ratios**, not cutting nurses outright.
Blames the **trust board and vendors**, not the technology itself.
Her concrete fear is a **wet bed** left forty minutes; she speaks from experience.
Learning only under **compulsion**, with help from Precious, the healthcare assistant.

steps.text: Push for a written staffing agreement before any AI is installed
Sit through the compulsory charting training with Precious helping
Raise monthly savings from one hundred to one fifty

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need laws, fast: no robot or AI making care decisions without a registered nurse responsible. I'd be out at the march, I'm not ashamed of that. And I'd say to friends, look, they still need hands, give it a minute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, two years is nothing. The charting, the care plans, the discharge planning, that's maybe a third of my shift, and that goes first. Then around 2031 the robots arrive for the washes and turns, and I'm thirty-two with no plan B because I never wanted one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd join the national campaign the union would run, and I'd write to my MP the same week. I'd stop the holiday we'd planned for next summer and put that money aside instead. And I'd ask Jonas whether we could move somewhere cheaper, closer to his mum, to stretch the savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly. I'd be scared and angry together, and I'm not good with change, so I'd probably freeze for the first month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The robots come about three years after the thinking AI here. What does that three-year gap mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'd have three years where the computer does the thinking and I do the washes and the lifting. That's three years of being the hands for a machine, which sounds miserable, but it's also three years of pay. I'd use it to save as much as I could and fight for rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years' warning, what would you do differently from the slower pictures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have no time to retrain into anything even if I wanted to, so I'd lean on the union and on family. With two years, the only thing I control is how much I save and how loud I am.

say: We need **laws fast**, with a registered nurse responsible for every care decision.
Wards still need **human hands**, at least for a few years.
think: Two years is **nothing**; a third of her shift is charting and planning.
Around **2031** the robots arrive for washes and turns.
At thirty-two she'd have **no plan B**, because she never wanted one.
do: Joins the **union's national campaign** and writes to her MP that week.
Cancels **next summer's holiday** and banks the money instead.
Talks with Jonas about **moving somewhere cheaper** near his mum.
feel: **Scared and angry** at the same time.
Expects to **freeze** for the first month.
S2.quote: Two years is nothing. The charting, the care plans, the discharge planning, that's maybe a third of my shift, and that goes first.
fieldNote: The **three-year gap** feels like being 'the hands for a machine'.
Sees **saving and protest** as the only levers with two years' warning.
Resistance to change means **no retraining plan** even under pressure.
Household relies on **two modest incomes**, so a move is on the table.

steps.text: Join the union's national campaign for nurse-led care rules
Write to her MP the same week about safe staffing law
Cancel next summer's holiday and put the money aside
Look at moving somewhere cheaper near Jonas's mum

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's use them to write the rules properly this time. Ratios in law, nurse sign-off on anything a machine decides. I'd say that loudly, at work and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is better than two, but I know myself. I'd spend three of them hoping it doesn't happen. By 2034, when the robots come for the hands-on work, I'd be thirty-five and still on Ward 7, probably.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my name down to be a union rep at branch level, not just the floor, because that's where the agreements get written. I'd save harder, maybe two hundred a month once the rent settles. And I'd probably do the palliative care course, because dying people will want a person, whatever happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less frozen than with two years. There's room to breathe, a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why palliative care in particular?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've sat with people at the end, holding a hand at three in the morning. I can't picture anyone wanting a robot for that, even if it could do it. It's the one bit of my job that I'd bet on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd spend three years hoping it doesn't happen. What would change your mind sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing it on my own ward. If the charting system suddenly started writing the care plans and the managers cut a post, I'd move straight away. Stories on the news don't move me, but Ward 7 would.

say: Five years is time to **write the rules** properly, with ratios in law.
Nurses should **sign off** on anything a machine decides.
think: She'd spend three years **hoping** it doesn't happen.
By **2034** she'd likely still be on the same ward at thirty-five.
do: Stands for **branch-level union rep**, where agreements are written.
Saves about **two hundred a month** once rent settles.
Takes the **palliative care course** as a safer specialism.
feel: **Anxious**, but with some room to breathe.
S3.quote: I've sat with people at the end, holding a hand at three in the morning. I can't picture anyone wanting a robot for that, even if it could do it.
fieldNote: Bets on **end-of-life care** as the most human part of nursing.
Admits she'd **delay acting** until change reaches her own ward.
Five years shifts her from **freezing to planning**, slowly.
Her politics stay steady: **ratios in law** and nurse sign-off.

steps.text: Stand for branch-level union rep at the city general
Save about two hundred a month once the rent settles
Enrol on the palliative care course run by the hospital

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this decently if governments actually bother. Train people, protect ratios, keep a nurse in charge. I'd say it in the union newsletter, probably.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels survivable. By 2039 I'd be forty, maybe senior, maybe in palliative care. I'd still be worried about the young ones coming in, but for me it's enough time to find a corner of nursing that stays human.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the palliative course in the first couple of years, slowly, while working. I'd keep the union stuff going. And I'd keep saving the hundred a month and not panic, because panicking with ten years to go is silly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but steady. It's like knowing the hospital will be rebuilt in a decade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a student nurse starting now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a student nurse to learn the bits nobody can measure: how to calm someone, how to spot that a patient is going off before the numbers do. And join the union on day one. That advice wouldn't change in any of your pictures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever use the AI tools yourself in that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they were properly tested and the union had signed off, then fine, I'd use them. I'm not against machines, I'm against being rushed. Ten years is not rushed.

say: Ten years is enough **to do this decently** if governments bother.
Train people, **protect ratios** and keep a nurse in charge.
think: Ten years feels **survivable** for her own career.
She worries more for the **young nurses** coming in.
She expects to find a **human corner** of nursing by forty.
do: Takes the **palliative course** slowly over the first two years.
Keeps her **union work** going alongside shifts.
Keeps saving **a hundred a month** without panicking.
feel: **Uneasy but steady**, like knowing a rebuild is ten years off.
S4.quote: I'm not against machines, I'm against being rushed. Ten years is not rushed.
fieldNote: The **decade** removes most of her fear for herself.
Would use tools once **union-approved**, a clear condition.
Advice to students centres on **unmeasurable skills** and union membership.

steps.text: Take the palliative care course part-time over two years
Keep working as union steward on Ward 7
Keep saving a hundred a month into the joint account

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. Two years is no time for someone like me who doesn't move quickly. What would help is a law on nurse-to-patient ratios that no software can override, and a proper pay rise so I've got more than two months in the bank.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the patients' families. They're the ones who'll be told a robot is caring for their mum, and they'll be furious. I'd want them on our side, because nurses alone get ignored.

headlineQuote: I don't blame the machine, I blame whoever signs the contract.
portrait: Freya is a **27-year-old ward nurse** on an older people's ward and her floor's union steward.
She distrusts **hospital IT** after years of systems that crash and double-book.
Her answers centre on **staffing ratios**, not AI itself, in every picture.
Two years' warning **frightens** her; ten years feels survivable with a palliative care move.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is too short for someone who changes slowly.
whatWouldHelp: A **ratio law** software can't override, plus a pay rise to grow her **savings**.
